findings.reason: The protected solution is concise, conventional, and interview-ready. The names unresolved, current, value, start, answer, and length expose the pending start indices, current scan position and value, resolved boundary, accumulated count, and suffix boundary directly. It has no exact generic local named index.

The stack contains exactly the start positions whose first strictly smaller later value has not yet appeared, with their values non-decreasing from bottom to top. When nums[current] is smaller than a stacked start value, all earlier scanned values were at least that start value, so current is its first invalid ending and precisely current - start valid subarrays begin there. Repeated popping resolves every larger start blocked by the same value. Equal values are deliberately retained because equality preserves validity. Each remaining start has no smaller value to its right and contributes length - start suffix endings, so every valid subarray is counted once and no invalid one is included.

Metadata consistently identifies Premium LeetCode problem 1063, Python, and the native validSubarrays(nums) interface. Authenticated source evidence confirms an integer array of length 1 through 50000 with values from 0 through 100000. The app-local solve adapter preserves non-empty contiguous-subarray counting, the requirement that the leftmost element be no larger than every later element, separate boundary-pair multiplicity, equality semantics, single-element validity, and the integer total return contract.

The protected app source and immutable native source bound to verified submission 2067467527 are algorithmically identical: both maintain the same stack of unresolved positions, pop only on a strictly smaller current value, add the same current-minus-start contribution, push every current position, and add the same suffix contributions for all remaining starts. Their only structural differences are the required Solution.validSubarrays wrapper and native typing syntax.

The three hidden workloads grow strictly increasing arrays from 32 through 512 elements, a 16x span, so every start remains valid to the end and a direct extension method examines every boundary pair while the monotonic stack still processes each position a constant number of times. The exact protected source passed all eleven visible correctness cases and all three performance tiers with relative growth exponent +0.01 and a 1.04x largest runtime ratio. An independently correct quadratic extension control matched every correctness and benchmark output but failed only the calibrated complexity verdict at +1.16 and 100.62x, distinguishing O(N) stack processing from O(N^2) enumeration.

The Approach accurately derives each start's first strictly smaller boundary, states the unresolved-stack invariant, explains why one current value may resolve several starts, preserves equality correctly, and accounts for unpopped suffix contributions. Its edge cases cover increasing, decreasing, duplicate, and singleton arrays. The O(N) time and O(N) auxiliary-space claims match the protected implementation and branch manifest.

The modular Reference preserves non-empty contiguous-subarray semantics, the leftmost-element condition with equality allowed, independent boundary-pair counting, singleton validity, all three source examples with their complete valid-subarray enumerations, both authenticated constraints, and both source hints. It includes the live 0 through 100000 element-value bound that the legacy document omitted. The live statement contains no images, diagrams, tables, notes, or follow-up section.

The authenticated live Premium statement directly verified exactly three examples in source order with exact arrays, outputs, and complete valid-subarray enumerations; contiguous non-empty semantics; the leftmost-value condition; two constraints; and two RMQ plus binary-search hints. source_fidelity.json binds those facts and every composed local section to the reviewed statement hash e7b8d40da3779c2500c2a156f318a754a0e103a7cbd3b316b492e29dd2f492a8.

coverage: The authenticated Premium statement contains exactly three examples. Their exact arrays and outputs appear first in source order, and the source explanations enumerate all 11 mixed-case subarrays, the three decreasing singletons, and all six equal-value boundary pairs.

All eleven ordinary correctness cases are visible samples or trials. They cover both length endpoints 1 and 50000, value endpoints 0 and 100000, singleton validity, equality at the leftmost minimum, and distinct subarrays with identical value sequences counted by their boundary pairs.

Material behavior includes a non-decreasing array where every subarray is valid, a decreasing array where only singletons survive, equal plateaus retained across equality, a later strict drop resolving several starts, valleys, alternating rises and drops, and maximum values blocked by a later minimum.

An independent direct-extension oracle fixes each start, extends rightward until the first strictly smaller value, and counts every earlier ending. It recomputed every authored expected value without using a monotonic stack or first-smaller-boundary aggregation.

The oracle, protected app source, and immutable native Solution agreed on all 14 authored correctness-plus-benchmark inputs, 21844 exhaustive arrays over values 0 through 3 up to length seven, 5000 deterministic random legal arrays, and five explicit boundary databases including the visible legal decreasing array at maximum length 50000.

The maximum-length visible case exposed the generic trace-step ceiling rather than an algorithm defect. A challenge-specific allowance now lets the accepted linear traversal finish, and a focused API regression proves the authored boundary case remains correct through the production runner.

The 32-, 128-, and 512-element increasing workloads remain hidden and performance-only, use size consistently as N, and span 16x. A correct O(N^2) direct-extension control matched every output and failed only scaling at +1.16 and 100.62x, while the O(N) protected source passed at +0.01 and 1.04x.
